name: Simón Bolívar
role: South American independence leader and president of Gran Colombia (1819–1830)
summary: Bolívar led independence campaigns against Spanish rule and promoted a confederation of the new Spanish American republics. He pursued emancipation and Indigenous land and labour reforms. He favoured a strong central executive and assumed supreme power in Gran Colombia in 1828.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Bolívar maintained the armed forces throughout his rule and made command of them a central function of the Colombian head of state.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: At Angostura Bolívar proposed a hereditary Senate. Article 149 of his later Bolivian draft abolished hereditary offices, privileges and entails.

abolish-ip.rationale: Article 151 of his Bolivian draft recognized inventors’ ownership of their creations and required temporary exclusive rights or compensation on disclosure.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: The Cúcuta and Cuzco decrees made wage contracts and payment enforceable for Indigenous labourers to replace compulsory and unpaid service.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: His land decrees recognized Indigenous owners of communal reserves and granted individual title in Peru. His 1829 forest regulations expressly recognized both publicly and privately owned forests.

allow-dual-citizenship.rationale: Article 18 of his Bolivian draft expressly removed citizenship rights upon taking foreign citizenship.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: Bolívar led armed resistance against the restoration of Spanish rule and issued the Declaration of Angostura rejecting a return to Spanish sovereignty.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: His 1828 decree assigned the collection and spending of public revenues to the head of state, who governed by decree until a new national assembly convened.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Article 10 of Bolívar’s draft constitution counted people born in Bolivian territory as Bolivians as well as specifying acquisition by descent.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: The 1813 War to the Death decree treated neutral Spanish and Canary Islander civilians as targets. The 1820 treaty committed Bolívar’s government to protecting the inhabitants of towns occupied by either side during the same war.

civilizational-union.rationale: As president of Colombia and later in Peru, Bolívar formally invited the countries of formerly Spanish America to confederate and establish a common assembly.

collective-defense.rationale: In Thoughts on the Congress to Be Held in Panama, Bolívar proposed that all members come to the aid of any member attacked by an outside enemy.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The Jamaica Letter condemned Spain for restricting American agriculture, manufacture and trade to protect the interests of the peninsula.

conscription.rationale: The Carúpano emancipation decree imposed military enlistment on able-bodied male freed people between fourteen and sixty.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Bolívar decreed the return of Indigenous reserve land and ordered additional allotments for Indigenous Peruvians dispossessed under Spanish rule.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: In his Cuzco land decree Bolívar expressly denied constitutional authority to caciques and assigned public authority to provincial and district officials.

death-penalty.rationale: Bolívar’s January 1824 decree prescribed death for officials convicted of misappropriating public funds at or above its specified threshold.

decide-locally.rationale: The Organic Decree placed prefects and provincial governors under the central executive and gave the head of state broad appointment and removal powers.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: His Bolivian draft empowered the legislature to elect the first president and gave succession to a vice president nominated by the incumbent and confirmed by the legislature.

dominated-front.rationale: Bolívar formally convened the governments of the former Spanish colonies to coordinate through a confederate assembly in the face of common dangers from Europe.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Bolívar’s constitutional draft barred Bolivia from becoming the patrimony of any family and made presidential succession run through the vice presidency.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Under the Organic Decree, Bolívar dispensed with the ordinary preliminary inquiry and written arrest order when public security required arrests in cases of offences against the state.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Bolívar backed standing alliances among the Spanish American republics and called a congress of their plenipotentiaries to consolidate them.

equal-conscription.rationale: The Carúpano decree mandated enlistment for able-bodied men of qualifying age and explicitly exempted women.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Organic Decree guaranteed equality before the law, and the Cuzco reforms prohibited unequal burdens on Indigenous citizens. His October 1828 resolution imposed a distinct personal tribute on Indigenous Colombians.

every-country-ready-for-democracy.rationale: In the Jamaica Letter Bolívar argued that representative institutions required political habits and experience that the Spanish colonies had been denied, and opposed instituting fully popular systems immediately.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Article 1 of the Organic Decree assigned command of the land and naval forces to the supreme head of state.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: The Cúcuta decree restored Indigenous communal reserves to their legitimate owners. In Peru his Cuzco decree converted community land into individual allotments and rejected the public authority of the caciques.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: At Angostura Bolívar argued that laws must fit the people and conditions of the society they govern and rejected copying the United States constitution for Venezuela.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Articles 10 and 14 of his Bolivian draft allowed foreigners to acquire nationality after three years or active citizenship after four years subject to qualifications.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Bolívar took military command in Peru to defeat the royalist forces and secure Peruvian independence while holding the Colombian presidency.

more-religion-public.rationale: The Organic Decree made the protection of Roman Catholicism a government duty. His Cúcuta decree required religious instruction in the schools it established.

national-church-status.rationale: Article 25 required the government to maintain and protect Roman Catholicism as the religion of Colombians.

national-resource-control.rationale: The Quito decree vested mineral deposits in the republic and regulated private mining concessions. His forest decree set public controls on the extraction of commercial timber and medicinal plants.

native-born-offices.rationale: Articles 14 and 16 of his Bolivian draft made naturalized foreigners eligible for citizenship and reserved public posts to active citizens rather than to the native-born.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Bolívar led armed defence of the independence republics and charged the Colombian head of state with defending the country against attack using its armed forces.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Bolívar issued decrees directing public authorities to organize schools, distribute land and regulate forest harvesting.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: His 1820 Cúcuta decree mandated that schools set up under provincial authority teach the principles of religion.

pay-off-national-debt.rationale: In his October 1825 letter to Peru’s finance minister Bolívar proposed transferring state assets and rights to companies or creditors to extinguish the national debt.

people-in-arms.rationale: The Cartagena Manifesto explicitly criticized the rejection of a standing army in favour of militias, which Bolívar held had failed to defend the republic.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Article 15 placed the administration of justice in a system of public courts exercising authority in the name of the republic.

property-franchise.rationale: In his speech to the Bolivian Congress he explicitly excluded a property test from the franchise and required literacy and an occupation instead.

property-fundamental.rationale: Article 21 of his Organic Decree declared property inviolable and permitted public use only in manifest and urgent necessity with just compensation.

racial-franchise.rationale: His Bolivian draft allowed people freed from slavery to become Bolivians and imposed the stated qualifications for political citizenship without limiting it to one ethnic group.

regional-resource-ownership.rationale: Article 1 of the Quito mining decree vested mines throughout Gran Colombia in the republic.

remove-indigenous-peoples.rationale: Bolívar ordered the restoration of Indigenous reserve lands and compensated Indigenous Peruvians whose land had been confiscated under colonial rule.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Bolívar led the independence revolution and, in the 1818 Declaration of Angostura, formally rejected any reconciliation that would restore Spanish rule.

separate-church-state.rationale: His 1828 Organic Decree established official protection for Catholicism and assigned the Council of State an advisory role in selecting senior church personnel.

state-harmful.rationale: Bolívar reorganized the Colombian state under a constitutional decree, retaining its courts, ministries, treasury and armed forces.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Bolívar required government protection of Catholic religious life and ordered religious and civic instruction in the schools organized under the Cúcuta decree.

strong-leader.rationale: After the Ocaña convention broke down, Bolívar assumed supreme power and gave the executive authority to issue decrees and amend or repeal laws.

students-direct-own-learning.rationale: His Cúcuta decree required children of specified ages to attend school and fixed the subjects they were to study.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Organic Decree assigned the Council of State a role in senior church appointments, and his 1820 decree put local priests’ compliance with rules on fees and sacraments under civil oversight.

suppress-opposition.rationale: In November 1828 Bolívar banned secret societies and instructed provincial officials to dissolve their meetings, a measure directed chiefly at lodges associated with his political opponents.

taxation-theft.rationale: Article 24 of the Organic Decree explicitly imposed a duty to contribute to public expenses in proportion to one’s fortune.

term-limits.rationale: In his 1826 constitutional proposal, Bolívar made the presidency a lifetime office and explicitly permitted senators to be reelected.

torture-always-illegal.rationale: Article 121 of Bolívar’s proposed Bolivian constitution barred torture and coerced confessions in criminal proceedings.

vote-at-sixteen.rationale: His Bolivian draft required voters to be married or above twenty-one, excluding unmarried sixteen-year-olds from the franchise.

widespread-small-property.rationale: His Cuzco decree distributed communal land in small individual plots to Indigenous citizens, including those who had previously lacked land.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The 1825 Cuzco decree granted Indigenous women the same individual land allotment as Indigenous men under the general distribution rule.

notes: Reviewed the historical record across economy, government, society, world affairs, liberty, culture, ecology, technology, political means and globalism. The Gutenberg author/title search found a biography by Guillermo A. Sherwell, not a work authored by Bolívar. Modern policy questions without equivalent positions in the sources remain unknown.
